To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of patients can resume oral feeding within 2 weeks after percutaneous gastrotomy tube placement.

the following factors are associated with a higher likelihood of resuming oral nutrition: (1) younger age; (2) lower body mass index; (3) higher serum albumin; (4) lower total protein; (5) higher serum sodium; and (6) lower serum potassium.

patients who are older than 60 years of age, have a low serum albumin level, and/or have a low preoperative body mass index are at higher risk of not resuming oral feeding following PEG tube placement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of the duration of enteral feeding.
the prediction of the time to resumption of oral nutrition after per cutaneous endoscopic gastro stomy tube placement.
the development of a method to predict which patients can resume normal oral nutrition after per cutaneous endoscopic gastro stomy tube placement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
patients who have a high likelihood of being able to resume oral feeding within 4–8 weeks of PEG placement are appropriate candidates for PEG placement.
the current evidence is not sufficient to support a recommendation for or against the use of any of these methods to predict when patients can resume oral intake.
there are no data to suggest that patients who have been tube-fed for 3 months or more have an increased mortality rate compared with those who were tube-fed for less than 3 months.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
patients with head and neck cancer who are expected to resume oral feeding are more likely to do so than patients with other diagnoses.
patients who have a percutaneous endo-scopic gastrostomy placed and who are expected to resume oral feeding should be followed closely for a minimum of 1 month.
the patients who were more likely to resume oral feeding were younger, had lower body mass indices, and had less severe illness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of death is low for patients who are able to resume oral nutrition and that the risk of aspiration pneumonia is low for all patients who resume oral nutrition.

patients who can resume oral nutrition are more likely to be older, have a shorter duration of hospital stay, be discharged to home, have a lower Charlson Comorbidity Index, and have a lower number of comorbidities.

patients with an intact swallowing mechanism, who have a history of aspiration, and who have a high risk of aspiration on the modified barium swallow are at high risk of developing aspiration pneumonia after percutaneous gastrostomy placement.
